chapter_title: Writing ROS Subscribers and Message Callbacks

screens.title: Writing ROS Subscribers and Message Callbacks
screens.subtitle: How nodes receive messages, process them in callbacks, and stay alive to handle events

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how ROS nodes receive messages and react to them automatically. A subscriber is a node that listens to a topic and hands incoming messages to a callback function you define. Callbacks let ROS deliver data efficiently without your code polling for updates. You will see how to write a Python subscriber, a C++ subscriber, and a combined subscriber–publisher node that transforms and republishes data. We also cover how the ROS event loop — implemented with rospy. spin() and ros::spin() — keeps a node alive and dispatches callbacks, and why queue sizes and callback speed matter for message delivery. Practical examples in Python and C++ show the exact patterns you will reuse in sensor pipelines and small data-processing nodes. By the end, you will understand how to handle single-threaded Python callbacks, threaded C++ callbacks, and when to use anonymous node names for multiple instances. Think of this as learning to open the mailbox reliably and process each letter without missing important information.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Subscribers receive messages and ROS calls your callback to process them; the event loop keeps the node alive and dispatches those callbacks.

narration.text: By the end of these screens you will be able to write working ROS subscribers in both Python and C++, explain how callbacks are scheduled, and keep nodes alive with the correct event-loop call. You will build a subscriber–publisher node that reads values from one topic, applies a deterministic transform, and republishes the result. These objectives emphasize practical skills: creating Subscriber objects, ensuring the callback can access and publish data, and controlling message buffering with queue_size. For Python, you will use rospy. Subscriber and understand why rospy. spin() is necessary to process messages. For C++, you will use nh. subscribe and learn how ConstPtr avoids copies for large messages. You will also practice running multiple instances with anonymous node names so each process has a unique identity in the ROS graph. Each objective is verified by building a small node and observing the output with rostopic echo. These are core competencies you will apply in sensor-processing pipelines and real robot systems.

narration.text: This second objectives screen focuses on verification and common pitfalls. You'll test Python and C++ subscribers by running sample publishers and observing rostopic echo output. For verification, the activity includes building a number_counter in Python that subscribes to /number and publishes a running count to /number_count. You will also implement a C++ string reverser that subscribes to /input_string and publishes reversed text to /output_string. These small projects verify that subscribers are receiving messages, callbacks run as expected, and publishers created inside the node publish reliably. Pay attention to garbage collection in Python: storing the Subscriber object in a variable prevents it from being collected. Also verify node uniqueness by using anonymous names when running multiple instances. The habit of testing with rostopic pub and rostopic echo will make debugging fast and clarify whether dropped messages are caused by queue limits, slow callbacks, or missing spin calls.

screens.title: What is a Subscriber and How Callbacks Work
screens.subtitle: The mailbox metaphor and the callback contract

narration.text: A subscriber is a node that receives messages published on a topic and processes them through a callback function you provide. Think of a subscriber as a mailbox and the callback as the person who opens and reads each letter. ROS handles the waiting for messages and calls your callback only when data arrives. This callback model avoids polling loops and reduces wasted C P U cycles. Concretely, the subscriber registers with the ROS Master and establishes connections to existing publishers. When a message arrives, ROS delivers the message object to your callback. In Python, callbacks execute in the main thread in the order messages arrive, so a slow callback will delay later messages. In C++, callbacks may run on separate threads depending on the spinner and node configuration. A common misconception is that subscribers actively fetch messages; they do not. ROS pushes messages into callbacks. Example: a camera publisher sends frames; a subscriber's callback receives each frame and immediately processes it. If your frame-processing is slow, frames may be dropped or buffered depending on queue_size and threading choices. Closing takeaway: design callbacks to be short or explicitly manage concurrency so your node keeps up with the incoming rate.

keyIdea.title: Subscriber contract
keyIdea.text: ROS pushes messages to your callback when they arrive; keep callbacks efficient or use buffering and threads to avoid lost or delayed processing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Subscriber & Callback
Definition

Subscriber and callback model

A subscriber registers for messages on a topic; the callback is executed by ROS when messages arrive.

Key points
  • ROS pushes messages to your callback; no polling required.
  • Python callbacks run sequentially in the main thread unless you use extra threading.
  • C++ can execute callbacks on separate threads with appropriate spinners.
Common misconception
Subscribers do not actively fetch data; ROS delivers messages for you. Expect that slow callbacks slow down subsequent processing in Python.
Key Takeaway

Design callbacks to be fast, or move heavy work out of the callback to avoid blocking message delivery.

Analogy

Mailbox and mail-handler

Mailbox (Topic)

Messages arrive here and wait for the subscriber to handle them.

Mail-handler (Callback)

Opens and processes messages when notified by ROS.

Example scenario
A camera publishes frames at 30 Hz. The subscriber's callback processes each frame. If processing takes 200 ms per frame, callbacks may fall behind unless you buffer or parallelize work.
Check your understanding
If your Python callback takes 5 seconds, what happens to incoming messages?
Pro tip
Keep only minimal logic in callbacks and hand off heavy work to background threads or queues.

narration.text: Let's walk through a Python subscriber example and explain each part you will reuse. The essential steps are: initialize the node with rospy. init_node, create a rospy. Subscriber with the topic name, message type, and callback function, keep a reference to the subscriber to avoid garbage collection, and call rospy. spin() so the node stays alive to process callbacks. In the example, the callback receives a message object and logs its data. The code registers the subscriber immediately with the ROS Master and ROS manages incoming message delivery. A typical mistake is to forget rospy. spin(); without it the script exits and the subscriber never handles messages. Another subtle detail is that Python callbacks execute sequentially in the main thread. If one callback takes a long time, later messages are held off. If you need concurrency, consider a worker thread or using message queues inside the callback. Use rostopic pub and rostopic echo when testing. Practice by publishing a few strings and confirming that the callback logs each incoming message. Writing a Python Subscriber means rospy.init_node, rospy.subscriber(topic, type, callback), keep subscriber object, then rospy.spin() to process callbacks.. In practical terms, rospy.subscriber, callback signature, and rospy.spin(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern to remember
keyIdea.text: rospy.init_node, rospy.Subscriber(topic, Type, callback), keep subscriber object, then rospy.spin() to process callbacks.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Python Subscriber
Code
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

def callback(msg):
  rospy.loginfo("Received: %s", msg.data)

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('robot_news_listener', anonymous=True)
  sub = rospy.Subscriber('/robot_news', String, callback)
  rospy.loginfo("Subscriber is ready. Waiting for messages...")
  rospy.spin()
This pattern shows node init, subscriber creation, logging, and spin to process callbacks.
Explanation
  • rospy.Subscriber registers the callback for messages on /robot_news.
  • Keep the returned subscriber in a variable to prevent garbage collection in Python.
  • rospy.spin() blocks and lets rospy process incoming messages and call callbacks.
Example
Publish a string with rostopic pub and watch the log from the callback showing Received: <message>.
Misconception
rospy.Subscriber does not block; spin is required to prevent the script from exiting immediately.
Key Takeaway

Follow the init → subscribe → spin pattern and keep callbacks brief or delegate heavy work.

screens.title: Writing a C++ Subscriber
screens.subtitle: nh.subscribe, callback signature, ConstPtr, and ros::spin()

narration.text: Now examine the C++ pattern for subscribers. The C++ example uses ros::init to initialize the node and a ros::NodeHandle to manage subscriptions. You call nh. subscribe with the topic name, a queue_size parameter, and the callback function. The callback receives a ConstPtr to the message, which is a shared pointer that avoids copying potentially large message payloads. This zero-copy behavior matters when working with images or point clouds. After creating the subscriber the node calls ros::spin() to enter the event loop and dispatch callbacks. Unlike Python's single-threaded default behavior, C++ can process callbacks on multiple threads when you use a MultiThreadedSpinner, allowing parallel handling of messages. A frequent mistake is forgetting to set a reasonable queue_size; a too-small queue causes recent messages to be dropped under load. Test your C++ subscriber by building and running the node, publishing messages, and watching the ROS_INFO log output in the console. Practice helps you internalize how ConstPtr and queue_size affect performance. Writing a C++ Subscriber means use nh.subscribe with a queue_size and constptr for efficient callbacks; use ros::spin() or a spinner to dispatch callbacks.. In practical terms, nh.subscribe, callback signature, constptr, and ros::spin(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: C++ subscriber focus
keyIdea.text: Use nh.subscribe with a queue_size and ConstPtr for efficient callbacks; use ros::spin() or a spinner to dispatch callbacks.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › C++ Subscriber
Code
#include <ros/ros.h>
#include <std_msgs/String.h>

void callback(const std_msgs::String::ConstPtr& msg) {
  ROS_INFO("Received: %s", msg->data.c_str());
}

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  ros::init(argc, argv, "robot_news_listener");
  ros::NodeHandle nh;

  ros::Subscriber sub = nh.subscribe("/robot_news", 10, callback);
  ROS_INFO("Subscriber is ready. Waiting for messages...");
  ros::spin();

  return 0;
}
Note the use of ConstPtr and queue_size. Build and run this node, then publish strings to /robot_news to see ROS_INFO output.
Explanation
  • ConstPtr provides a shared pointer to the message without copying data.
  • queue_size sets how many messages to buffer before dropping old ones.
  • ros::spin() processes incoming messages until shutdown.
When to use multithreading
If callbacks perform heavy work, a MultiThreadedSpinner in C++ allows parallel callback execution and reduces message loss due to slow handlers.
Key Takeaway

C++ offers efficient zero-copy access through ConstPtr and configurable buffering via queue_size; pick a spinner strategy that matches your processing needs.

screens.title: The ROS Event Loop: rospy.spin() and ros::spin()
screens.subtitle: How the node stays alive and dispatches callbacks

narration.text: The ROS event loop is the mechanism that keeps your node alive and delivers incoming messages to callbacks. In Python you call rospy. spin(), and in C++ you call ros::spin(); both functions block the main thread and let ROS process incoming events until shutdown. Consider spin as the node's waiting room: it keeps the process alive and dispatches callbacks when messages arrive. Without spin, your script will continue past subscriber creation and may terminate before any callbacks have run. It's important to realize that spin itself does not process heavy work; it simply dispatches callbacks into your execution environment. In Python, callbacks are invoked sequentially in the main thread while spin is active. That means a long-running callback will delay subsequent callbacks. In C++, ros::spin() can work with MultiThreadedSpinner to execute callbacks on multiple threads for parallelism. When designing nodes, decide whether callbacks should be short synchronous handlers or whether they should enqueue work for background processing. Testing with rostopic pub and watching callback logs will confirm that spin is working and callbacks are being invoked as expected. The ROS Event Loop: rospy.spin() and ros::spin() means call spin to keep the node alive and allow ros to deliver messages to your callbacks; choose single-threaded or multi-threaded behavior to match processing needs.. In practical terms, how the node stays alive and dispatches callbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event-loop summary
keyIdea.text: Call spin to keep the node alive and allow ROS to deliver messages to your callbacks; choose single-threaded or multi-threaded behavior to match processing needs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Event Loop
Process

Blocking spin keeps the node alive

rospy.spin() and ros::spin() block and let ROS dispatch callbacks until the node is shut down. They are essential to keep subscribers responsive.
Python behavior
Callbacks run sequentially in the main thread; slow callbacks block later ones.
C++ behavior
Callbacks may be executed on multiple threads with a MultiThreadedSpinner, allowing parallel handling.
Checklist
  • Always call spin after creating subscribers to keep the node alive.
  • If callbacks are slow, offload work to threads or use a multi-threaded spinner in C++.
  • Test with rostopic pub and rostopic echo to ensure callbacks are invoked.
Why it matters
Without a running event loop, subscribers never process messages; this leads to silent failures that are hard to debug unless you check for spin behavior.
Key Takeaway

Spin is the mechanism that dispatches callbacks; choose a threading model that fits your processing demands.

screens.title: Callback Execution: Python vs C++
screens.subtitle: Sequential callbacks in Python, threaded callbacks in C++ and buffer trade-offs

narration.text: This screen compares how callbacks are executed in Python and C++ and why that matters for message throughput and latency. In Python with rospy, callbacks run sequentially in the main thread: ROS delivers a message, waits for your callback to finish, then moves to the next message. This simple model is easy to reason about but susceptible to delays when a callback is slow. In C++, callbacks can run on separate threads depending on the spinner you choose, enabling parallel processing of messages. That reduces latency when you have C P U-bound work in each callback but also introduces concurrency concerns such as shared state protection. Another related concern is buffering: the subscriber's queue_size determines how many messages ROS will buffer before dropping the oldest or newest messages depending on configuration. A small queue can drop messages when callbacks are slow; a large queue accumulates messages that may become stale. Concrete example from the chapter: a callback that takes 5 seconds with a publisher at 1 Hz will let two messages be processed in 10 seconds, but depending on queue_size many intermediate messages will be dropped or buffered. The practical conclusion is to choose a spinner and buffer size that matches your processing latency and to design callbacks to avoid holding up the pipeline.

keyIdea.title: Execution contrast
keyIdea.text: Python runs callbacks serially; C++ supports multi-threaded callbacks. Pick buffer sizes and threading to match processing time and message rates.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Callback: Python vs C++
Python

Sequential callbacks

Callbacks run in the main thread and are invoked in arrival order. A single slow handler delays subsequent callbacks.

Misconception
Python callbacks are not automatically parallel; they run one after another unless you create your own threads.
Tip

Use worker threads from callbacks if you must handle long-running tasks.

C++

Threaded callbacks possible

With a MultiThreadedSpinner, callbacks can run concurrently on multiple threads, improving throughput for CPU-bound handlers but requiring thread-safe code.

Queue and buffering
queue_size controls how many messages are buffered. If callbacks are slower than incoming rate, messages will be dropped when the buffer is full.
Concrete example

A 5-second callback and 1 Hz publisher result in two processed messages in 10 seconds; queue_size affects how many intermediate messages are retained or dropped.

screens.title: Subscriber–Publisher Node: Number Counter (Python)
screens.subtitle: Subscribe, update state, and publish transformed data

narration.text: A common pattern is a node that both subscribes and publishes. The number counter example demonstrates this: the node subscribes to /number, maintains an internal count, increments it for each received message, and publishes the new count on /number_count. This pattern shows how callbacks can update node state and use a Publisher created in the same node. Important practical points: create the Publisher in the node's constructor or initialization so it's ready when callbacks run; increment internal state inside the callback and then publish the transformed message; and ensure rospy. spin() keeps the node alive. The provided Python class holds state in self. count and references both self. sub and self. pub so nothing is garbage collected. When testing, run a number publisher that emits Int64 messages and verify the output with rostopic echo /number_count. This pattern is the basis for filters, aggregators, and many processing nodes in ROS and highlights the need to keep callback work bounded or offload heavy computation to background workers. Subscriber–Publisher Node: Number Counter (Python) means use a persistent publisher and update internal state in the callback to produce transformed outputs for downstream nodes.. In practical terms, subscribe, update state, and publish transformed data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Subscriber–publisher pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a persistent Publisher and update internal state in the callback to produce transformed outputs for downstream nodes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Subscriber→Publisher
Code
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import Int64

class NumberCounter:
  def __init__(self):
    self.count = 0
    self.sub = rospy.Subscriber('/number', Int64, self.callback)
    self.pub = rospy.Publisher('/number_count', Int64, queue_size=10)

  def callback(self, msg):
    self.count += 1
    count_msg = Int64()
    count_msg.data = self.count
    self.pub.publish(count_msg)
    rospy.loginfo("Received: %d, Count: %d", msg.data, self.count)

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('number_counter', anonymous=True)
  node = NumberCounter()
  rospy.spin()
This class-based node keeps state and ensures the publisher is available to callbacks.
Explanation & Example
Run a number publisher that sends Int64 values. Each incoming message increases the internal counter and publishes the updated count to /number_count for verification with rostopic echo.
Why this pattern is useful
This pattern lets nodes act as filters, aggregators, or converters in a pipeline of transformations, where each node performs a single, testable task.
Key Takeaway

Create the publisher early, update state inside callbacks, and use rostopic echo to confirm published results.

screens.title: Anonymous Node Names and Multiple Instances
screens.subtitle: Why anonymous=True or AnonymousName matters for scalability

narration.text: Anonymous node names make it simple to run many instances of the same node without name collisions. In Python, passing anonymous=True to rospy. init_node appends a random suffix to the node's name so each process is unique on the ROS graph. In C++ you achieve the same effect with ros::init_options::AnonymousName. This is critical when you have multiple identical sensors or processors running on the same machine or network; otherwise, nodes that share a name may conflict and cause registration issues with the ROS Master. A common confusion is expecting unique node names by default. If you run multiple copies without anonymous naming, each new instance tries to register with the same name and can cause unexpected behavior. Practically, use anonymous names for per-sensor nodes or multi-instance testing, and use stable names when you need to discover nodes by name. When testing, observe rosnode list to confirm each instance has a unique name. This simple change makes deployments and scaling of homogeneous nodes much safer. Anonymous Node Names and Multiple Instances means use anonymous node names when running multiple identical instances to avoid name collisions on the ros master.. In practical terms, why anonymous=true or anonymousname matters for scalability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Naming practice
keyIdea.text: Use anonymous node names when running multiple identical instances to avoid name collisions on the ROS master.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Anonymous Nodes
Definition

Anonymous node names

Append a random suffix to node names so multiple instances can run without colliding on the ROS master.

Python
rospy.init_node('sensor_reader', anonymous=True)
C++
ros::init(argc, argv, "sensor_reader", ros::init_options::AnonymousName)
Why use it
Run many identical nodes, each with a unique name, so they register independently.
When not to use
If other components discover nodes by a stable name, avoid anonymous naming.
Validation
Check rosnode list to see unique instance names like sensor_reader_12345.
Key Takeaway

Anonymous names are essential for scalable deployments of identical nodes; use stable names when needed for discovery.

screens.title: Message Buffering and the queue_size Assessment
screens.subtitle: How queue_size affects drops when callbacks are slow

narration.text: This lesson walks through the assessment example and shows the role of queue_size. Scenario: a subscriber's callback takes five seconds to process each message, while a publisher sends messages at 1 Hz. First, with queue_size set to 1, ROS buffers a single message. When a callback is busy, new incoming messages cause the buffer to hold the most recent message while older ones are dropped depending on the transport behavior. In ten seconds the publisher sends ten messages, but the slow callback processes only two messages — one at t=0 and another at t=5 — because each callback consumes five seconds. With queue_size set to 10, ROS can buffer up to ten messages; in ten seconds it receives ten messages and still processes only the two callbacks, leaving eight messages in the buffer. The core insight is that buffering cannot increase processing throughput for a single-threaded slow consumer; it only delays when messages are dropped or how stale buffered messages become. To truly increase processed messages, you must reduce processing time, parallelize work, or slow the publisher. When designing systems, choose queue_size to balance memory, acceptable staleness, and drop behavior under load.

keyIdea.title: Buffering insight
keyIdea.text: queue_size controls buffering but cannot compensate for a slow callback; increase throughput by parallelizing or reducing processing time.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › queue_size & Assessment
Assessment scenario

Slow callback and publisher rate

Publisher at 1 Hz, callback takes 5 seconds. Compare queue_size 1 and queue_size 10.

queue_size = 1
Node processes 2 messages in 10 seconds (at t=0 and t=5). Intermediate messages are dropped; only the most recent buffered message survives while the callback is busy.
queue_size = 10
Node still processes 2 messages in 10 seconds, but up to 8 messages accumulate in the buffer. Those buffered messages may become stale if processing doesn't catch up.
Practical guidance
Buffering helps when short bursts cause temporary overload, but it does not increase long-term throughput. To handle steady overload, reduce processing time or parallelize work.
Key Takeaway

queue_size affects buffering but cannot overcome a slow single-threaded consumer; address the bottleneck in processing or change the producer rate.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's recap the most important concepts. First, a subscriber registers with the ROS Master and receives messages on a topic; ROS pushes those messages into your callback. Second, use rospy. Subscriber in Python and nh. subscribe in C++; in C++ prefer ConstPtr for large messages to avoid copies. Third, call rospy. spin() or ros::spin() to keep the node alive so callbacks can be dispatched; choose a multithreaded spinner in C++ when you need parallel callbacks. Fourth, queue_size controls buffering but cannot increase processing throughput for a slow consumer; to handle high rates, reduce processing time or parallelize. Finally, anonymous node names let you run multiple instances without name conflicts. These concise reminders will help you debug and design subscriber-based nodes effectively. Practice by building the number_counter and string_reverser examples and verifying behavior with rostopic pub and rostopic echo.

keyIdea.title: Core reminders
keyIdea.text: Subscribers + callbacks + spin form the reactive core of ROS; design callbacks and buffering to meet your data rate and latency needs.

Summary takeaway
Use the subscriber–callback pattern with careful attention to callback duration, buffering, and the appropriate spinner for your language to build reliable ROS pipelines.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three one-line reminders to carry forward

narration.text: To finish, hold on to three crisp reminders: 1) Subscribers hand incoming messages to callbacks defined by you; design those callbacks to be quick or to offload heavy work. 2) Always call rospy. spin() or ros::spin() so callbacks can be dispatched; consider multi-threaded spinners in C++ for parallelism. 3) Use anonymous node names to run many instances, and set queue_size to balance buffering and acceptable staleness. Practically, test with rostopic pub and rostopic echo, and watch logs to confirm callbacks run. These three rules cover most debugging scenarios you will face when building sensor pipelines and processing nodes in ROS. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means keep callbacks short or parallelize, call spin to enable callbacks, and choose anonymous names and queue sizes thoughtfully.. In practical terms, three one-line reminders to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Keep callbacks short or parallelize, call spin to enable callbacks, and choose anonymous names and queue sizes thoughtfully.
